script.opening: (Mother, exasperated, close to tears; Maisie not in view.) "I'm at the end of my tether, doctor. Maisie keeps dirtying her pants — proper soiling — at school and at home. She's 5, she's toilet-trained, so I think she's either being lazy or doing it on purpose for attention. The school have mentioned it. I've tried telling her off but it makes no difference. What do I do with her?"

facts.text: "Not every day. When she goes it's hard, sometimes huge. She cries sometimes" — every 4–5 days, "like pellets or a big log", once blocked the toilet. Some blood on the paper once when it was very hard.
"Now you say it, yes. She seems to hold on, then says she doesn't need to go" — crosses her legs, hides behind the sofa, goes red in the face.
"Soft, smeary. She says she didn't know. I thought she was lying." Most days for about 3 months. Smells.
Fully toilet-trained at 3. Hard poos started around starting school (about 9 months ago) — doesn't like the school toilets. "I'm not sure about school — she doesn't like to talk about it."

"No, nothing like that. She's always been healthy and she's growing fine." Passed meconium on day 1. No vomiting, no swollen tummy, no leg weakness or walking problems, no back problems, wees normally, no wetting. Red book weights on track.
Fussy eater: pasta, chicken nuggets, yoghurts; little fruit or veg. Drinks mostly milk (3 cups a day) and squash.
No medicines tried apart from prune juice once. No allergies. Lives with Mum (works in a supermarket) and older brother (9). Dad sees her at weekends. No social worker.
If asked how she's coping: "Honestly, I feel like a bad mum. The school look at me like I'm not coping. And I keep telling her off, which I feel awful about."

Frustrated and blaming at first. Softens when the doctor explains overflow: "So she really didn't know? … That's a relief, the internal bit." Dismayed at the warning: "Worse? Right before I'm back at the school gate?" Accepts a school letter gratefully. If the doctor just tells her to be firmer, agrees and asks for a reward chart (the trap).

ice.ideas: "She's lazy or doing it for attention."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — feeling judged by the school as a bad mum; guilt about telling Maisie off; exhausted.
ice.expectations: "Tell me how to make her stop."

cues: "She says she didn't know." — the overflow clue.
"I feel like a bad mum." — guilt to relieve.

checkpoints.text: REFRAMES the soiling as OVERFLOW INCONTINENCE from chronic constipation/impaction (involuntary, the child usually cannot feel it) — NOT laziness or naughtiness — and removes blame as a therapeutic first step

Takes a focused history (Bristol stool form, withholding behaviour, painful/hard or very large stools, palpable mass, diet/fluids, toileting, onset/triggers) and arranges a face-to-face examination (abdomen, perianal inspection, spine/lower limbs, growth), as it cannot be done by video

EXCLUDES red flags for organic disease (NICE CG99: from-birth onset, delayed meconium >48h, gross distension with vomiting, neurological/spinal signs, ribbon stools) and would refer if present, treating faltering growth as amber (test for coeliac disease and hypothyroidism)

Manages per NICE CG99 with DISIMPACTION FIRST — escalating osmotic macrogol (dose per BNFC; add a stimulant if not disimpacted after 2 weeks) titrated over ~1–2 weeks — and WARNS that soiling/abdominal pain may temporarily worsen during disimpaction (not a reason to stop)
Plans MAINTENANCE laxatives continued for months (not stopped too soon) plus behavioural measures (post-meal toilet sitting, footstool, reward for sitting, fluids/fibre, school-toilet access)
Reframes compassionately for both child and mother, relieves blame/guilt, and addresses the punitive dynamic — protecting the child from shame
Sets realistic expectations (this takes months) and checks the mother’s understanding so she adheres rather than stopping early

Safety-nets and follows up: review of disimpaction/maintenance, what to expect, when to return (red flags, no improvement), and ongoing support — evidence-based, de-shaming care with any emotional/safeguarding impact considered

worked.txt: "I can hear how exhausting this is — but here’s the key thing: Maisie almost certainly isn’t being naughty or lazy. This is what happens when a child gets very constipated: hard poo backs up, and softer poo leaks around it without her feeling it or being able to stop it. She genuinely can’t control it."

"Let me ask — when she does poo, is it hard or painful, or really big? Does she hold on, cross her legs, or avoid the toilet? Does her tummy feel hard? … That fits a backed-up bowel causing the soiling."

"A few checks: was she constipated from birth, slow to pass her first stool as a newborn, growing well? Any tummy swelling or back/leg problems? … All reassuring so far — this sounds like the common, treatable type, and I’ll check her tummy, bottom, back and growth when I see her in person this week."

"We clear the backlog first with a laxative powder, building the dose up over a couple of weeks. Important: her soiling and tummy ache might get WORSE for a few days as it clears — that’s expected, it means it’s working, so don’t stop."

"Once cleared, she stays on a daily dose for months to keep poos soft — we don’t stop early or it comes straight back. Plus sitting on the toilet after meals with a footstool, a star chart just for sitting, and plenty of fluids and fibre."

"Please go easy on her — telling off makes it worse and she can’t help it. This takes patience, often months. Come back if she’s not improving, develops tummy swelling, blood, or weight loss, and let’s review how she’s getting on."

f.learning: Involuntary soiling in a previously toilet-trained child is almost always OVERFLOW INCONTINENCE from chronic constipation with faecal impaction — hard stool builds up, the rectum stretches, and softer stool leaks around it without the child feeling it or being able to control it — so the crucial, therapeutic first step is to REFRAME it as a medical problem, not laziness, naughtiness or deliberate behaviour, removing the blame and shame that worsen it. Take a focused history (Bristol stool form, withholding behaviour, painful/hard or very large stools, palpable abdominal mass, diet/fluids, toileting routine, school-toilet avoidance, onset/triggers) and arrange a face-to-face examination of the abdomen, perianal area, spine and lower limbs with growth plotted (it cannot be done by video, and no digital rectal examination in primary care), while EXCLUDING NICE CG99 red flags for organic disease (symptoms from birth, delayed passage of meconium beyond 48 hours suggesting Hirschsprung’s, gross abdominal distension with vomiting, abnormal lower-limb neurology/spinal signs, ribbon stools) which would prompt referral; faltering growth is an amber flag prompting tests for coeliac disease and hypothyroidism. Manage per NICE CG99 with DISIMPACTION FIRST using an escalating osmotic macrogol (e.g. Movicol Paediatric Plain), titrated up over about 1–2 weeks (dose per BNFC, adding a stimulant if not disimpacted after 2 weeks), and warn the family that soiling and abdominal pain may temporarily worsen as the backlog clears — this is expected and not a reason to stop, since under-dosing or stopping early is the commonest cause of apparent failure. Follow with MAINTENANCE laxatives continued for several months (not stopped abruptly once improved, as relapse is common) plus behavioural measures — regular post-meal toilet sitting using the gastrocolic reflex, a footstool for positioning, a reward chart for sitting rather than results, adequate fluids and fibre, and addressing school-toilet avoidance — with de-shaming throughout. The hidden agenda is parental frustration, exhaustion and a misunderstanding of the mechanism, often with guilt under the anger; reframe compassionately for both child and mother, set realistic month-long expectations, protect the child from shame, and watch for emotional/safeguarding impact.

knowledge.guideline: NICE CG99 (2010, updated 2017) — Constipation in children and young people · NICE CG89 — Child maltreatment: when to suspect
knowledge.summary: Soiling in a toilet-trained child is overflow from faecal impaction until shown otherwise. Remove the blame, screen for red flags, then disimpact before maintenance and continue treatment for months.

points.t: Hard stool loads the rectum, the rectum stretches and loses sensation, and softer stool leaks around it. The child usually cannot feel it or stop it. Saying so clearly is the first treatment.

NICE CG99: stool frequency and form (Bristol scale), pain or straining, large stools, withholding behaviour, overflow soiling, onset and triggers (toilet training, starting school, a fissure), diet and fluids, and growth.

NICE CG99: constipation from birth or the first few weeks, meconium passed more than 48 hours after birth in a term baby, ribbon stools, abnormal lower-limb neurology or spine, gross distension with vomiting, abnormal anus. Faltering growth is an amber flag — test for coeliac disease and hypothyroidism. No digital rectal examination in primary care.

NICE CG99: macrogol (polyethylene glycol 3350 with electrolytes) in an escalating dose as first line (dose per BNFC). Add a stimulant laxative if it has not worked after 2 weeks. Warn the family that soiling and tummy pain may increase at first.

NICE CG99: continue the maintenance dose for several weeks after a regular bowel habit is established, then reduce gradually. Many children need laxatives for several months. Do not use dietary change alone as first-line treatment.

NICE CG99: scheduled toileting, a bowel diary, and rewards for agreed behaviours such as sitting on the toilet, not for clean pants. NICE CG89 applies if there are wider concerns about maltreatment or punitive responses.

dg.d: Open question; let mother voice her frustration and her theory of laziness or attention-seeking without interrupting.
School involvement and toilet avoidance, family stress, punitive responses, the mother’s guilt and coping.
Face-to-face abdominal and perianal inspection, spine and lower-limb check, growth plotted; no digital rectal examination; no routine tests.
Functional constipation with overflow versus organic causes (Hirschsprung’s, spinal, coeliac, hypothyroidism) and emotional triggers.
CG99 red flags: from-birth onset, delayed meconium, ribbon stools, neurology, distension with vomiting; faltering growth as amber.
Functional constipation with faecal impaction and overflow soiling, explained in plain language.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Escalating macrogol disimpaction (dose per BNFC), warning of temporary worsening, maintenance for months, scheduled toileting and rewards for sitting.
School-toilet access letter, fluids and diet as adjuncts not first-line, possible fissure, emotional impact on the child.
Review two weeks after starting; add a stimulant if not disimpacted; named red flags; do not stop early.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

Idea (behavioural); concern (being judged as a bad mother, guilt about telling her off); expectation (make her stop).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.

model.text: Hello Mrs Cobb, thanks for calling. Tell me what’s been going on with Maisie.
model.why: Open question; lets the frustrated parent speak first

model.text: I’m at the end of my tether. She keeps dirtying her pants — at school and at home. She’s 5, she’s toilet-trained, so she’s either being lazy or doing it for attention. The school have mentioned it. Telling her off does nothing.

That sounds exhausting, and having the school involved makes it harder. I want to understand it properly, because there’s often a very physical reason behind this. Can I ask some questions about her bowels, then explain what I think and make a plan with you?
model.why: Validates, hints at a medical explanation and sets the agenda

model.text: Go on.
When she does a proper poo on the toilet, what is it like — hard, big, painful? And how often does she go?
model.why: Stool form and frequency — the core of the CG99 history

model.text: Not every day. When she goes it’s hard, sometimes huge. She cries sometimes.
Does she ever seem to hold on — crossing her legs, standing stiffly, hiding, or refusing to sit on the toilet?
Now you say it, yes. She seems to hold on, then says she doesn’t need to go.
And the soiling itself — is it soft or smeary rather than a full poo? Does she seem to notice when it happens?
Soft, smeary. She says she didn’t know. I thought she was lying.

I’d also like to check a few things from when she was small. Did she have problems with her bowels from birth, or was there any delay passing her first poo as a newborn? Has she been growing normally? Any swollen tummy with vomiting, or problems with her legs or walking?
No, nothing like that. She’s always been healthy and she’s growing fine.
What’s her eating and drinking like, and how does she get on with the toilets at school?
I’m not sure about school — she doesn’t like to talk about it.
You said she might be doing it for attention. What else has been going through your mind about it?
model.why: Explores the parent’s idea and what sits beneath the anger

model.text: Honestly, I feel like a bad mum. The school look at me like I’m not coping. And I keep telling her off, which I feel awful about.
Thank you for being so honest. You’re clearly trying hard, and anyone would be worn down by this. What were you hoping I’d be able to do today?
model.why: Responds to guilt without judgement and elicits expectations

model.text: Tell me how to make her stop.

Here’s the key thing: I don’t think Maisie is being naughty or lazy at all. When a child gets constipated, hard poo builds up and stretches the end of the bowel. It stops sending the “I need to go” message, and softer poo leaks around the blockage without her feeling it. She genuinely can’t control it.
model.why: The central reframe: overflow from impaction, not behaviour

model.text: So she really didn’t know?

She really didn’t. And the hard poos hurt, so she holds on, which makes the next one harder — it’s a cycle, not a choice. The good news is it’s very common and very treatable. I’d like to see her in person this week to feel her tummy, look at her bottom for any small tear, check her back and plot her growth. I won’t need to do an internal examination.
model.why: Explains the pain-withholding cycle and arranges the examination the video cannot do

model.text: That’s a relief, the internal bit.

Treatment has two stages. First we clear the blockage with a laxative powder mixed into a drink, starting low and building up each day until it clears. Now, an important warning: for the first few days the soiling and tummy ache may get worse. That means it’s working — please don’t stop.
model.why: Disimpaction first, with the CG99 warning about temporary worsening

model.text: Worse? Right before I’m back at the school gate?
I know — so it might help to start at the weekend, and I can write a note for school explaining it’s a medical problem and she needs easy access to the toilet. Would that help?
model.why: Responds to a practical barrier and involves school supportively

model.text: Yes, that would really help.

Second stage: once she’s cleared, she stays on a daily dose to keep her poos soft — usually for months, not weeks, and we reduce it slowly. Stopping early is the commonest reason it comes back. Alongside that, sitting on the toilet for a few minutes after meals with her feet on a small step, and a sticker chart for sitting — not for clean pants, because that part isn’t in her control yet.
model.why: Maintenance for months plus behavioural measures that reward behaviour, not outcome

model.text: And no more telling her off, I suppose.
That would help her most. Praise for sitting, no blame for accidents. Could Maisie hear some of this from me too, so she knows it isn’t her fault?
model.why: Protects the child from shame and involves her positively

model.text: Yes, I think she’d like that.
Before we finish, can you tell me in your own words what the plan is?
Clear-out first, building up the powder, it may get worse for a few days. Then a daily dose for months. Toilet after meals with a step, sticker chart for sitting. No telling off.

Exactly. I’ll see her this week to examine her and go through the doses, then review two weeks after starting. Contact us sooner if she has tummy pain with vomiting, a swollen tummy, blood in her poo, weight loss, or if the clear-out hasn’t worked after two weeks.
model.why: Specific safety-net, review points and escalation if disimpaction fails

model.text: Thank you. I came in thinking she was being difficult.
You came in because you care about her, and you did the right thing. We’ll get there together — it takes patience, but it works.
model.why: Closes with hope and realistic expectations

social.t: Toilet avoidance at school is a common trigger. A letter explaining the medical problem and asking for easy toilet access and discreet help with changing supports treatment and reduces shame.
Soiling strains parent–child relationships. Punitive responses worsen withholding; the plan should reduce conflict at home.

legal.t: NICE CG89: consider maltreatment where there are wider concerns — punitive or humiliating responses, or an unexplained change in behaviour. Here, the repeated telling off calls for support and education; escalate only if concerns persist or grow.

professional.t: Share information with school with the parent’s consent and only what is needed (GMC Confidentiality, 2017).
Explain to Maisie at her level that it is not her fault. Children’s views should be sought in decisions about them (GMC 0–18 years guidance).

community.t: School nurse and health visitor or continence services can support toileting programmes. ERIC, The Children’s Bowel and Bladder Charity, provides family resources.

redFlags: Constipation from birth or first weeks; meconium delayed beyond 48 hours in a term baby (Hirschsprung’s)
Ribbon stools, gross distension with vomiting, abnormal leg neurology or spine, abnormal anus
Faltering growth (amber — coeliac and thyroid tests); concerns about maltreatment
psychosocial: School toilet avoidance and the school’s response
Punitive responses at home and the mother’s guilt
Impact on Maisie’s confidence and friendships
ice: Idea: “She’s being lazy or doing it for attention”
Concern: being seen as a bad mother; guilt about telling her off
Expectation: “Tell me how to make her stop”

playbook.diagnosis: Functional constipation with faecal impaction and overflow soiling. No red flags on history; confirm on examination (abdomen, perianal inspection, spine, growth) without a digital rectal examination.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Hard poo has built up and stretched the end of her bowel, so it stops telling her when she needs to go. Softer poo leaks around it without her feeling it. It isn’t naughtiness — she can’t control it.”

management.reflectIce: “You thought she was doing it on purpose — and it’s completely understandable you felt that. What she told you, that she didn’t know, is actually the truth, and that’s good news because it means it’s fixable.”
management.psychosocial: Lift blame from both mother and child; plan disimpaction around school; offer a school letter; replace telling off with praise for sitting.
sharedPlan: Escalating macrogol disimpaction (dose per BNFC); warn soiling may worsen briefly
Maintenance macrogol for months, reduced gradually; stimulant if disimpaction fails at 2 weeks
Toilet sitting after meals with a footstool; rewards for sitting; fluids and diet alongside
safetyNet: Review two weeks after starting, then regularly through maintenance
Return sooner for vomiting, distension, blood in the stool, weight loss or failure to clear

pitfalls.intro: This station is about a reframe. Candidates who know the macrogol regimen still fail if they let the “naughty” framing stand, skip the red flags, or send the family away with a treatment that is set up to fail.

items.fail: Offering parenting strategies for “behavioural” soiling without taking a bowel history.
items.why: Missing overflow from impaction is a diagnostic failure; the history that makes it takes two minutes.
items.fix: Ask about hard or large stools, pain, withholding and whether she notices the soiling — then name overflow.

items.fail: Correcting the mother bluntly: “She’s not naughty, she’s constipated.”
items.why: It lands as blame on the parent, who then disengages. The anger covers guilt and feeling judged.
items.fix: Validate first, explore what she has been thinking, then explain the mechanism using her own observations.

items.fail: Starting a low daily laxative dose without disimpacting.
items.why: NICE CG99 puts disimpaction first. A maintenance dose in a loaded rectum increases leakage and the family abandons treatment.
items.fix: Escalating macrogol until cleared, then maintenance — and warn that soiling may worsen at first.

items.fail: No red-flag screen, or a plan to do a rectal examination.
items.why: CG99 red flags must be asked; digital rectal examination is not done in primary care.
items.fix: From-birth onset, meconium, ribbon stools, growth, distension with vomiting, legs and back — then inspect, don’t examine internally.

items.fail: Saying the laxatives can stop “once she’s better”.
items.why: Relapse after early stopping is the commonest cause of treatment failure; examiners look for realistic timescales.
items.fix: “Months, not weeks — and we’ll reduce slowly together.”

items.fail: Talking only to the mother about Maisie as a problem.
items.why: A child who has been told off repeatedly needs to hear it is not her fault; ignoring her misses a protective step.
items.fix: Offer to explain to Maisie directly, and recommend praise for sitting and no blame for accidents.

timeMap.d: Let the frustration out. Don’t correct “lazy” yet — gather the evidence first.
Stool form and frequency, pain, withholding, soft smeary soiling she doesn’t notice. From-birth onset, meconium, growth, distension, legs and back. Diet, fluids, school toilets.
What else has she been thinking? Guilt and feeling judged sit under the anger.
Overflow, not naughtiness. Examine in person. Disimpact first with the warning, then maintenance for months, toilet sitting and rewards for sitting.
Her words for the plan. Review at two weeks; red flags; school letter.

wordPics.fail: Accepts the behavioural framing or gives parenting tips; no bowel history; no red-flag screen; starts a low maintenance dose in an impacted child with no warning of worsening; no plan for how long to continue.
wordPics.pass: Takes a focused bowel history, screens red flags, explains overflow, prescribes macrogol disimpaction then maintenance, gives toileting advice and a follow-up.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: uses mother’s own words (“she says she didn’t know”) to reframe; responds to her guilt; warns of temporary worsening and plans around school; stresses months of maintenance; rewards behaviour not outcome; involves Maisie so she hears it is not her fault.

avoid.dont: “Have you tried a star chart for clean pants?”
avoid.instead: “A sticker for sitting on the toilet after meals — the clean pants will follow once the bowel recovers.”
avoid.why: Rewarding an outcome the child cannot control adds failure and shame.

avoid.dont: “Give her more fruit and water and it should sort itself out.”
avoid.instead: “We need to clear the blockage with medicine first — diet helps alongside, but on its own it won’t shift it.”
avoid.why: NICE CG99 advises against dietary change alone as first-line treatment.

avoid.dont: “Stop the laxative once she’s clean for a week.”
avoid.instead: “She’ll stay on a daily dose for months, and we’ll reduce it slowly together.”
avoid.why: Stopping early is the commonest cause of relapse.

SCA_MODELS.why: Disimpaction first, with the CG99 warning about temporary worsening

SCA_MODELS.text: Worse? Right before I’m back at the school gate?
I know — so it might help to start at the weekend, and I can write a note for school explaining it’s a medical problem and she needs easy access to the toilet. Would that help?
SCA_MODELS.why: Responds to a practical barrier and involves school supportively

SCA_MODELS.text: Yes, that would really help.

Second stage: once she’s cleared, she stays on a daily dose to keep her poos soft — usually for months, not weeks, and we reduce it slowly. Stopping early is the commonest reason it comes back. Alongside that, sitting on the toilet for a few minutes after meals with her feet on a small step, and a sticker chart for sitting — not for clean pants, because that part isn’t in her control yet.
SCA_MODELS.why: Maintenance for months plus behavioural measures that reward behaviour, not outcome

SCA_MODELS.text: And no more telling her off, I suppose.
That would help her most. Praise for sitting, no blame for accidents. Could Maisie hear some of this from me too, so she knows it isn’t her fault?
SCA_MODELS.why: Protects the child from shame and involves her positively

SCA_MODELS.text: Yes, I think she’d like that.
Before we finish, can you tell me in your own words what the plan is?
Clear-out first, building up the powder, it may get worse for a few days. Then a daily dose for months. Toilet after meals with a step, sticker chart for sitting. No telling off.

Exactly. I’ll see her this week to examine her and go through the doses, then review two weeks after starting. Contact us sooner if she has tummy pain with vomiting, a swollen tummy, blood in her poo, weight loss, or if the clear-out hasn’t worked after two weeks.
SCA_MODELS.why: Specific safety-net, review points and escalation if disimpaction fails

SCA_MODELS.text: Thank you. I came in thinking she was being difficult.
You came in because you care about her, and you did the right thing. We’ll get there together — it takes patience, but it works.
SCA_MODELS.why: Closes with hope and realistic expectations

SCA_STEM.name: Maisie Cobb
pmh: No significant past medical history recorded
SCA_STEM.recent: Soiling at school and at home. The school has raised it with her mother. Telling her off has made no difference.
SCA_STEM.reason: Mother wants advice on how to stop Maisie “dirtying her pants”.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE CG99 (2010, updated 2017) — Constipation in children and young people · NICE CG89 — Child maltreatment: when to suspect
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Soiling in a toilet-trained child is overflow from faecal impaction until shown otherwise. Remove the blame, screen for red flags, then disimpact before maintenance and continue treatment for months.

points.t: Hard stool loads the rectum, the rectum stretches and loses sensation, and softer stool leaks around it. The child usually cannot feel it or stop it. Saying so clearly is the first treatment.

NICE CG99: stool frequency and form (Bristol scale), pain or straining, large stools, withholding behaviour, overflow soiling, onset and triggers (toilet training, starting school, a fissure), diet and fluids, and growth.

NICE CG99: constipation from birth or the first few weeks, meconium passed more than 48 hours after birth in a term baby, ribbon stools, abnormal lower-limb neurology or spine, gross distension with vomiting, abnormal anus. Faltering growth is an amber flag — test for coeliac disease and hypothyroidism. No digital rectal examination in primary care.

NICE CG99: macrogol (polyethylene glycol 3350 with electrolytes) in an escalating dose as first line (dose per BNFC). Add a stimulant laxative if it has not worked after 2 weeks. Warn the family that soiling and tummy pain may increase at first.

NICE CG99: continue the maintenance dose for several weeks after a regular bowel habit is established, then reduce gradually. Many children need laxatives for several months. Do not use dietary change alone as first-line treatment.

NICE CG99: scheduled toileting, a bowel diary, and rewards for agreed behaviours such as sitting on the toilet, not for clean pants. NICE CG89 applies if there are wider concerns about maltreatment or punitive responses.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question; let mother voice her frustration and her theory of laziness or attention-seeking without interrupting.
School involvement and toilet avoidance, family stress, punitive responses, the mother’s guilt and coping.
Picked up “she says she didn’t know” and “I thought she was lying” and used them to reframe.
Idea (behavioural); concern (being judged as a bad mother, guilt about telling her off); expectation (make her stop).
Face-to-face abdominal and perianal inspection, spine and lower-limb check, growth plotted; no digital rectal examination; no routine tests.
Functional constipation with overflow versus organic causes (Hirschsprung’s, spinal, coeliac, hypothyroidism) and emotional triggers.
CG99 red flags: from-birth onset, delayed meconium, ribbon stools, neurology, distension with vomiting; faltering growth as amber.
Functional constipation with faecal impaction and overflow soiling, explained in plain language.
Escalating macrogol disimpaction (dose per BNFC), warning of temporary worsening, maintenance for months, scheduled toileting and rewards for sitting.
School-toilet access letter, fluids and diet as adjuncts not first-line, possible fissure, emotional impact on the child.
Review two weeks after starting; add a stimulant if not disimpacted; named red flags; do not stop early.

social.t: Toilet avoidance at school is a common trigger. A letter explaining the medical problem and asking for easy toilet access and discreet help with changing supports treatment and reduces shame.
Soiling strains parent–child relationships. Punitive responses worsen withholding; the plan should reduce conflict at home.

legal.t: NICE CG89: consider maltreatment where there are wider concerns — punitive or humiliating responses, or an unexplained change in behaviour. Here, the repeated telling off calls for support and education; escalate only if concerns persist or grow.

professional.t: Share information with school with the parent’s consent and only what is needed (GMC Confidentiality, 2017).
Explain to Maisie at her level that it is not her fault. Children’s views should be sought in decisions about them (GMC 0–18 years guidance).

community.t: School nurse and health visitor or continence services can support toileting programmes. ERIC, The Children’s Bowel and Bladder Charity, provides family resources.

redFlags: Constipation from birth or first weeks; meconium delayed beyond 48 hours in a term baby (Hirschsprung’s)
Ribbon stools, gross distension with vomiting, abnormal leg neurology or spine, abnormal anus
Faltering growth (amber — coeliac and thyroid tests); concerns about maltreatment
psychosocial: School toilet avoidance and the school’s response
Punitive responses at home and the mother’s guilt
Impact on Maisie’s confidence and friendships
ice: Idea: “She’s being lazy or doing it for attention”
Concern: being seen as a bad mother; guilt about telling her off
Expectation: “Tell me how to make her stop”

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Functional constipation with faecal impaction and overflow soiling. No red flags on history; confirm on examination (abdomen, perianal inspection, spine, growth) without a digital rectal examination.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Hard poo has built up and stretched the end of her bowel, so it stops telling her when she needs to go. Softer poo leaks around it without her feeling it. It isn’t naughtiness — she can’t control it.”

management.reflectIce: “You thought she was doing it on purpose — and it’s completely understandable you felt that. What she told you, that she didn’t know, is actually the truth, and that’s good news because it means it’s fixable.”
management.psychosocial: Lift blame from both mother and child; plan disimpaction around school; offer a school letter; replace telling off with praise for sitting.
sharedPlan: Escalating macrogol disimpaction (dose per BNFC); warn soiling may worsen briefly
Maintenance macrogol for months, reduced gradually; stimulant if disimpaction fails at 2 weeks
Toilet sitting after meals with a footstool; rewards for sitting; fluids and diet alongside
safetyNet: Review two weeks after starting, then regularly through maintenance
Return sooner for vomiting, distension, blood in the stool, weight loss or failure to clear

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is about a reframe. Candidates who know the macrogol regimen still fail if they let the “naughty” framing stand, skip the red flags, or send the family away with a treatment that is set up to fail.

items.fail: Offering parenting strategies for “behavioural” soiling without taking a bowel history.
items.why: Missing overflow from impaction is a diagnostic failure; the history that makes it takes two minutes.
items.fix: Ask about hard or large stools, pain, withholding and whether she notices the soiling — then name overflow.

items.fail: Correcting the mother bluntly: “She’s not naughty, she’s constipated.”
items.why: It lands as blame on the parent, who then disengages. The anger covers guilt and feeling judged.
items.fix: Validate first, explore what she has been thinking, then explain the mechanism using her own observations.

items.fail: Starting a low daily laxative dose without disimpacting.
items.why: NICE CG99 puts disimpaction first. A maintenance dose in a loaded rectum increases leakage and the family abandons treatment.
items.fix: Escalating macrogol until cleared, then maintenance — and warn that soiling may worsen at first.

items.fail: No red-flag screen, or a plan to do a rectal examination.
items.why: CG99 red flags must be asked; digital rectal examination is not done in primary care.
items.fix: From-birth onset, meconium, ribbon stools, growth, distension with vomiting, legs and back — then inspect, don’t examine internally.

items.fail: Saying the laxatives can stop “once she’s better”.
items.why: Relapse after early stopping is the commonest cause of treatment failure; examiners look for realistic timescales.
items.fix: “Months, not weeks — and we’ll reduce slowly together.”

items.fail: Talking only to the mother about Maisie as a problem.
items.why: A child who has been told off repeatedly needs to hear it is not her fault; ignoring her misses a protective step.
items.fix: Offer to explain to Maisie directly, and recommend praise for sitting and no blame for accidents.
